extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's 'The Rising Sea')
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter excerpt (Vakil) giving constructions, definitions, and exercises about the Grassmannian, relative Spec and Proj, and projective morphisms, including technical hypotheses, universal properties, and geometric consequences. Contains many exercises that state precise criteria/conditions and hints for proofs/constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representability of the Grassmannian functor via open subfunctors
rubrics_metrics.description: To show the Grassmannian functor G(k,n) is representable, cover it by open subfunctors G(k,n)_I indexed by k-subsets I ⊂ {1,...,n} where the corresponding k sections of Q are linearly independent (i.e., the determinant of the k×k matrix of the I columns is nowhere zero).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the statement precise locally: in a trivializing open neighborhood of Q the surjection φ: O^{⊕ n} → Q can be viewed as an n×k matrix M; the locus where the determinant of the k×k submatrix given by columns I is nowhere zero defines G(k,n)_I. Show this locus behaves well under transitions between trivializations. Use Exercise 10.1.H (Zariski sheaf + cover by representable opens) to deduce representability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine chart description G(k,n)_{ {1,...,k} } ≅ A^{k(n−k)}
rubrics_metrics.description: The open subfunctor G(k,n)_{ {1,...,k} } is represented by A^{k(n−k)}: after arranging the first k summands to give identity on the subbundle, the remaining columns are arbitrary linear combinations with functions a_{ij} giving coordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given a surjection φ: O^{⊕ n} → Q with φ1,...,φk forming a basis on the open, write each φ_j (j>k) as φ_j = a_{1j}φ1 + ... + a_{kj}φk. The k(n−k) functions a_{ij} on B correspond to a map B → A^{k(n−k)}. Conversely, given functions a_{ij} define the surjection. (See Exercise 16.4.C and Exercise 7.6.E.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric properties of Grassmannian (smoothness, irreducibility, dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Over a field, the Grassmannian is smooth and irreducible of dimension k(n−k); over any base the Grassmannian is smooth over that base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from covering by affine spaces A^{k(n−k)} and standard smoothness results (A^m is smooth). See reference to §13.6.2 and use that A^{k(n−k)}_B is smooth over B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tautological exact sequence on the Grassmannian
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a tautological exact sequence 0 → S → O^{⊕ n} → Q → 0 on G(k,n), where Q is the tautological quotient bundle and S the tautological subbundle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the universal object: points of the Grassmannian correspond to rank-k quotients of O^{⊕ n}, giving the universal surjection and its kernel. Use this exact sequence when forming determinant/Plücker maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plücker embedding via wedge^k
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying ∧^k to the universal surjection φ: O^{⊕ n} → Q gives ∧^k φ: O^{⊕ (n choose k)} → det Q, hence a map P: G(k,n) → P^{(n choose k)-1} (Plücker embedding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A surjection from a rank N free sheaf to a line bundle corresponds to a map to P^{N−1} (Theorem 15.2.2). Use Exercise 14.2.V to justify ∧^k φ and Yoneda's lemma / functoriality to obtain the induced map of representing schemes (Exercise 16.4.D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of Plücker coordinates and pullback of standard opens
rubrics_metrics.description: The projective coordinate x_I on P^{(n choose k)-1} may be interpreted as the determinant of the map φ_I: O^{⊕ k} → Q consisting of summands indexed by I; the standard open U_I (where x_I ≠ 0) pulls back to the affine open G(k,n)_I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the determinant interpretation precise: x_I corresponds to determinant of the I-columns minor. Show that PI: G(k,n)_I → U_I is a closed embedding by explicit coordinate maps: send the affine coordinates x_{I'}/x_I to determinants of k×k submatrices expressed in the a_{ij} (Exercise 16.4.E–G).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plücker (quadratic) equations cut out the Grassmannian
rubrics_metrics.description: There are quadratic relations (Plücker equations) among the k×k minors (Plücker coordinates) satisfied by G(k,n); for example, G(2,4) ⊂ P^5 is cut out by x12 x34 − x13 x24 + x14 x23 = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the quadratic relations hold on G(k,n) (Exercise 16.4.I,J) and note that these equations generate the homogeneous ideal of G(k,n) (proof requires additional work, see reference [F1]). For small cases (e.g., G(2,4)) check directly that the quadric defines the image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action of GL_n on the Grassmannian
rubrics_metrics.description: The group scheme GL_n acts on G(k,n); this is most easily described using the functor-of-points language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the functorial nature of the Grassmannian construction (compare Exercise 7.6.S(a) and Exercise 15.2.N) to show GL_n acts on the family of k-quotients of O^{⊕ n} by change of basis on O^{⊕ n}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction and representability of Grassmannian bundles G(k,F)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a rank-n locally free sheaf F on X, the Grassmannian bundle G(k,F) over X parametrizes k-dimensional quotients of fibers of F; it is representable and behaves well under base change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the functor and then prove representability by gluing the affine charts constructed over affines (Exercise 16.4.M). The construction is stable under base change (functorial/local nature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative Spec of a quasicoherent sheaf of algebras (universal property)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a quasicoherent sheaf of O_X-algebras R on a scheme X, Spec R → X is characterized by the universal property: X-morphisms (µ: W → X) → Spec R correspond functorially to O_X-algebra maps α: R → µ_* O_W making the evident diagram commute (17.1.2.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On affines Spec A ⊂ X with R|_{Spec A} = R, Spec R|_{Spec A} is the usual Spec R. Use this to glue and to show existence (Exercise 17.1.B). The universal property determines Spec R up to unique isomorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine-local computation and base-change compatibility of Spec
rubrics_metrics.description: Spec R can be computed affine-locally on X; formation of Spec commutes with base change (Exercise 17.1.F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use that over Spec A the construction is the usual Spec of an A-algebra and glue via Proposition 17.1.3. For a morphism Z → X, Z ×_X Spec R ≅ Spec (µ^* R) naturally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization: affine morphisms are Spec of pushforward algebra
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism µ: Z → X is affine iff Z ≅ Spec µ_* O_Z as X-schemes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show if µ is affine then µ_* O_Z is a quasicoherent O_X-algebra and Z ≅ Spec of this algebra. Conversely, Spec R → X is affine by construction (Exercise 17.1.D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of categories for Spec R
rubrics_metrics.description: For µ: Spec R → X, the category of quasicoherent sheaves on Spec R is equivalent to the category of quasicoherent R-modules on X (Exercise 17.1.E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the pushforward/pullback adjunction and the algebra structure of R to identify module structures; this is useful when X is simple but Spec R complicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total space of a locally free sheaf as Spec(Sym• F^∨)
rubrics_metrics.description: The total space (vector bundle) associated to a locally free sheaf F of rank n is Spec(Sym• F^∨); locally it is isomorphic to A^n_U and its sheaf of sections is F (17.1.4, 17.1.G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show local triviality by choosing local frames and use transition functions to recover F as global sections of the total space. Note some authors define the dual convention (Spec Sym• F vs Spec Sym• F^∨).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tautological line bundle O(−1) on P^n as a total space
rubrics_metrics.description: Over a field k, the subset X ⊂ P^n_k × A^{n+1}_k of pairs (line l, vector v on that line) gives π: X → P^n_k which is the line bundle corresponding to O(−1) (Exercise 17.1.H).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work on standard affine opens of P^n and compute transition functions to identify O(−1). The projection X → A^{n+1}_k at the origin relates to the blow-up of A^{n+1}_k.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative Proj construction and gluing from affines
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a quasicoherent graded O_X-algebra S satisfying reasonable hypotheses, Proj_X S is constructed by glueing the usual Proj of Γ(U,S) over affine opens U ⊂ X using compatibility data (Exercises 17.2.A–C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the explicit affine base-change isomorphism Proj_B(S⊗_A B) ≅ Proj_A S ×_{Spec A} Spec B to check compatibility. Exercise 17.2.B gives the general gluing method from data on an affine basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses for useful relative Proj (Hypotheses 17.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Proj to behave well, require S_0 = O_X, S is generated in degree 1 (i.e., the natural map Sym•_OX S1 → S is surjective), and S1 is finite type (finite generation in degree 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These conditions can be checked affine-locally. The generation-in-degree-1 condition ensures existence of an O(1) line bundle and nicer geometric behavior; one may relax them if necessary but must track consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of O(1) on Proj_X S under finiteness hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Hypotheses 17.2.1 (S0 = OX, generation in degree 1, S1 finite type) one can construct an invertible sheaf O_Proj_X S(1) that restricts to the standard O(1) on each affine Proj (Exercise 17.2.D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the local Proj constructions on affines and glue the canonical O(1) line bundles; the Sym•-generation hypothesis is used to ensure this gluing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proj commutes with base change
rubrics_metrics.description: For ρ: Z → X and S a graded quasicoherent algebra on X, there is a natural isomorphism Proj_Z(ρ^* S) ≅ Z ×_X Proj_X(S) compatible with O(1) (Exercise 17.2.E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the natural isomorphism and check O(1) pulls back appropriately (ψ^* OProj S(1) ≅ OProj ρ^*S(1)). Use the affine base-change statement (17.2.A) as the local ingredient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative projectivization PF = Proj(Sym• F)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a finite type quasicoherent sheaf F on X, the projectivization PF := Proj(Sym• F) is the relative projective bundle; if F is locally free of rank n+1 then PF is a P^n-bundle (17.2.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PF behaves well under base change and generalizes earlier notions of projective space; for locally free F of rank n+1, PF ≅ P(F) and coincides with previous constructions (cf. Exercise 4.5.Q).

rubrics_metrics.name: π-very ample (relative very ample) line bundle
rubrics_metrics.description: For a proper morphism π: X → Y, an invertible sheaf L on X is π-very ample if X = Proj_Y S for some graded quasicoherent algebra S on Y satisfying Hypotheses 17.2.1 and with L ≅ O(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defines relative very ampleness by presentation as a Proj with the given line bundle identified with O(1). See Exercise 17.2.F for maps of graded sheaves and Exercise 17.2.G for twisting by line bundles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twisting Proj by a line bundle (effect on O(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: If S is generated in degree 1 and L is an invertible sheaf on X, define S' = ⊕_n (S_n ⊗ L^{⊗ n}); then Proj S' ≅ Proj S as X-schemes, but O(1) is twisted by L (Exercise 17.2.G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informally, the underlying Proj is the same but the tautological O(1) changes by tensoring with β^* L. Use this to modify presentations so that desired line bundles correspond to O(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of projective morphism (Grothendieck style)
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π: X → Y is projective if there exists a quasicoherent graded O_Y-algebra S satisfying Hypotheses 17.2.1 (finite generation in degree 1) such that X ≅ Proj_Y S as a Y-scheme (Section 17.3.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: this definition does not require specifying O(1), so projectivity is not manifestly affine-local on the target without extra hypotheses. Grothendieck's definition is more general than some others (e.g., Hartshorne).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent characterization of projective morphisms via closed embeddings
rubrics_metrics.description: π: X → Y is projective iff there exists a finite type quasicoherent sheaf S1 on Y and a closed embedding i: X ↪ P_{S1} over Y (Exercise 17.3.A(a)). With a chosen invertible sheaf L and O(1) ≅ L, the same holds with i^* O(1) ≅ L (Exercise 17.3.A(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Exercise 17.2.H to construct the projective ambient space from S1. If Y admits an ample line bundle M, tensor S1 by a high power of M to obtain embeddings into P^n_Y (Exercise 17.3.A(c)); use Theorem 16.2.2 on finite generation of global sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasiprojective morphism (relative notion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Y is quasicompact, π: X → Y is quasiprojective if X is a quasicompact open subscheme of some scheme projective over Y (Section 17.3.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This notion is delicate in full generality (see EGA references); the textbook does not use quasiprojective heavily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability properties: base change, properness, and composition conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Projective morphisms are preserved under base change and are proper (hence separated, finite type, universally closed). Composition of projective morphisms is projective provided the final target is quasicompact (Exercise 17.3.B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For composition use the criterion of closed embedding into projective bundles (Exercise 17.3.A) and construct Segre-type embeddings/diagrams of projective bundles; handle affine case then glue for general Z (hint in 17.3.B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancellation theorem and related consequences for projective morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X → Y is a morphism and ρ: Y → Z is projective, then π ◦ ρ projective implies π is projective under suitable separatedness/projective-diagonal hypotheses (Exercise 17.3.C). Also, a morphism from a projective k-scheme to a separated k-scheme is projective (Exercise 17.3.D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the diagrammatic hints provided (cf. Exercise 11.2.A and Theorem 11.2.1) and the existence of projective embeddings to prove cancellation-type statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite morphisms are projective (and closed embeddings are projective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any finite morphism Z → X is projective: construct a graded O_X-algebra S with S0 ≅ O_X and Sn ≅ B (the finite algebra) for n>0 so that Z ≅ Proj S (Exercise 17.3.F). Consequently, closed embeddings are projective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows the chain closed embedding ⇒ finite ⇒ projective ⇒ proper, and provides an explicit graded algebra construction to realize finite maps as Proj.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative global generation and base-point-freeness
rubrics_metrics.description: For a quasicompact quasiseparated morphism π: X → Y and quasicoherent F on X, F is relatively globally generated (with respect to π) if the natural map π^* π_* F → F is surjective. A line bundle L is relatively base-point-free if it is relatively globally generated (Section 17.3.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the stated hypotheses π_* π^* F is quasicoherent and the condition is affine-local on Y. In proper/Noetherian/projective settings π_* L is often finite type (Grothendieck Coherence); if π is quasicompact separated, L relatively base-point-free and π_* L finite type then there is a canonical morphism ψ: X → P_π(π_* L) (Exercise 17.3.G), generalizing base-point-free maps to projective bundles.
